sections.overview: The large flying fox is a fruit-eating bat of tropical Southeast Asia and one of the world’s largest bats. Its fox-like face, pointed ears and broad wings distinguish it from small insect-eating bats. It roosts by day in trees and leaves after dusk to feed, sometimes crossing national borders between feeding areas and roosts.
sections.identification: Adults have a forearm about 180–220 mm long, a wingspan commonly reported near 1.5 m, and a mass of roughly 0.6–1.1 kg. A dark mantle covers the head and shoulders; its tones range from reddish mahogany to nearly black, while the underside is also often dark. The long fingers support a thin wing membrane, and clawed thumbs and hind feet help the bat cling to branches. Fur colour varies with age and sex.
sections.habitat: The species uses lowland tropical forest, mangroves, swamps, river margins, islands and, in some places, orchards and cultivated landscapes. Day roosts are often in tall trees, including mangroves and coconut groves. In a Malaysian field study, roosts were occupied seasonally as well as continuously, so a temporarily empty tree site did not by itself show that the colony had disappeared.
sections.diet: Fruit is the principal food, supplemented by flowers, nectar and pollen. The bat can use its teeth to open fruit and its long tongue to take soft pulp or liquid nectar. It searches for food at night with vision and smell; unlike echolocating insect hunters, it relies on sight rather than laryngeal echolocation for flight navigation. Local food choices vary with what is fruiting or flowering.
sections.behavior: Large flying foxes gather in conspicuous tree roosts, where individuals hang head-down and may spread or wrap their wings around the body. Colonies can shift between roosts, and counts fluctuate over time. Satellite tracking in Peninsular Malaysia documented long nocturnal feeding flights and movements between Malaysia, Sumatra and Thailand. These observations came from a small, male-biased sample, so they do not describe every animal’s routine. Field and captive studies also describe a social hierarchy; colonies may contain smaller harems centred on one male, although that grouping should not be assumed at every roost.
sections.reproduction: Females generally produce one pup in an annual breeding cycle, although timing differs by region. Reports place births in March or early April in Thailand and in April–May in the Philippines; these dates should not be treated as universal. A newborn is furred and open-eyed but still depends on its mother. She carries it during the first days, then leaves it at the roost while foraging; nursing continues for about two to three months.
sections.ecology: A field diet study at Subic Bay examined droppings of the Philippine subspecies P. vampyrus lanensis: Ficus seeds occurred in 66% of its samples, and Ficus variegata seeds in 34%. This shows that seeds pass through this bat’s gut, although it does not by itself prove successful seedling establishment. Fruit and flower feeding can move plant material, but the species-specific effects on pollination and forest regeneration remain incompletely measured.
sections.conservation: Hunting and loss or degradation of roosting and feeding habitat threaten populations. A 2003–2006 Peninsular Malaysian study counted at least 21,600 bats across surveyed roosts and estimated licensed hunting at about 22,000 per year in 2002–2005; its population models suggested that this level could be unsustainable. Those are historical, regional findings, not current range-wide counts. The global IUCN Red List category changed from Near Threatened to Endangered in the 2022 update. In the separate Peninsular Malaysia Mammal Red List of 2017, it was categorized regionally as Endangered.
